paper_title: OverSeer: Multi-Agent World Models Beyond What Agents See

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: World models aim to learn predictive representations of environments. Video world models represent the environment as sequence of images captured from the viewpoint of an acting agent, predicting future frames conditioned on past observations and agent actions. By taking advantage of large video datasets, these models can learn to represent complex visual dynamics and interactions between characters and objects. Recent video world models have made substantial progress in visual fidelity and character controllability, but maintaining coherent world over long horizons remains challenging. Small prediction errors can accumulate over time, causing objects to drift and environments to change inconsistently. These challenges become more pronounced in multi-agent environments. multi-agent world model must represent not only how the environment evolves but also how multiple characters interact within the same shared world. We identify two forms of consistency that are essential for this setting. First, world consistency requires persistent scene elements and the effects of past events to be preserved over time: when an agent revisits location, the scene should reflect its history. Second, agent consistency requires the actions and states of different agents to agree across their observations: an interaction should be depicted consistently in all views from which it is visible. These constraints are difficult to satisfy using only player-centric streams, because each player observes only partial and changing projection of the underlying world. One way to address these challenges is to use world-centric representation that explicitly maintains shared state independent of any individual agents viewpoint. Such representations can also model dynamics more efficiently: localized updates occur only when the environment actually changes, whereas an agents camera motion drastically alters egocentric pixels even in completely static scene. However, explicitly reconstructing and maintaining world-centric representation from partial observations remains challenging. In this paper, we propose video-based framework that captures the key advantages of world-centric representation without requiring explicit global state reconstruction. To this end, we introduce OverSeer, multi-agent video world model augmented with fixed-pose auxiliary camera views that serve as practical proxy for shared world-centric state. At inference, the auxiliary views are automatically, jointly, and efficiently generated with the agents views through shared attention. This design has three benefits: (i) Auxiliary views cover regions beyond individual agents immediate fields of view, establishing shared visual reference that grounds cross-agent interactions; (ii) Because the auxiliary cameras are stationary, any temporal variation in their views reflects actual environmental changes rather than camera ego-motion; (iii) Fixed viewpoints make temporal redundancies predictable and easy to model, reinforcing structural coherence across streams. To minimize computational overhead and exploit this inherent temporal redundancy, we introduce δ-VAE, variational autoencoder that performs second-stage latent compression on top of standard video VAE. For each auxiliary stream, δ-VAE retains an initial reference frame latent and encodes subsequent frames into compact residual latents conditioned on that reference. The static reference frame preserves persistent background geometry, enabling the residual latents to concentrate exclusively on dynamic events, such as agent movements, object manipulations, and environmental state changes. By eliminating redundant encoding of unchanged background content, six auxiliary views incur only 37.5% of the token overhead of the two agent streams. We evaluate OverSeer on Minecraft and Doom, two games with substantially different visual dynamics, spatial structures, and interaction patterns, and additionally show qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures (Shapovalov et al., 2023). When agents lose sight of each other and later reunite, existing multi-agent world models restore the partner or the scene correctly in only 012.5% of episodes, whereas OverSeer does so in 3860%, at small fraction of the cost of modeling the auxiliary views as full video streams.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Video Diffusion and Video World Models. Diffusion models have emerged as the dominant framework for video generation, evolving from early techniques that augmented pretrained 2D priors with temporal layers (Singer 2 et al., 2023; Blattmann et al., 2023) to large-scale architectures scaled for high-fidelity synthesis (OpenAI, 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025; HaCohen et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025). Video world models extend this paradigm by casting environment simulation as action-conditioned video diffusion, where future frame generation is guided by past observations and agent actions to yield interactive simulators (Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025). Recent full-stack systems further enrich this formulation by integrating explicit camera control, scene memory, and real-time streaming (DreamX et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). However, progress in this domain mainly focuses on expanding the input conditioning space, while output generation remains restricted to rendering single egocentric stream for single agent. In contrast, OverSeer shifts focus to the models output space: given initial frames and actions from all agents, the model jointly predicts every agents egocentric stream alongside the fixed auxiliary camera views, improving both world and agent consistency. Long-Horizon Consistency and Memory. Autoregressive rollouts in video world models tend to compound error and spatial drift over extended horizons (Chen et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). The prevailing remedy is expanding context capacity through positional extrapolation or streaming attention (Yang et al., 2026; Yesiltepe et al., 2026), memory-bank retrieval by estimated camera pose (Yu et al., 2025a; Hong et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026), and geometry-guided retrieval (DreamX et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). However, these memory structures are constructed entirely from an agents own past observations. Consequently, unobserved regions are never stored, and retrieval accuracy remains bound to pose estimates that drift alongside generation. Our pose-fixed auxiliary views serve complementary function: while memory recalls previously observed regions, auxiliary streams provide active coverage of unobserved space. Furthermore, because these auxiliary views are jointly predicted rather than retrieved, they eliminate reliance on fragile pose estimation altogether. Multi-Agent and Multi-View World Models. Multi-agent world models were first studied in reinforcement learning with compact state spaces (Egorov and Shpilman, 2022; Zhang et al., 2025), where multi-view consistency is enforced within an unrendered latent state. Recent work extends this requirement to the pixel domain, conditioning video diffusion models on multiple action streams to synthesize concurrent agent views (Enigma, 2025; Savva et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Hu et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026b). Multi-view generation also appears in generative 3D modeling and autonomous driving (Kong et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026b; Jang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2024a,b,c), though cameras in these settings are typically in static scene or camera rigs rigidly attached to single moving platform. Existing approaches to multi-agent consistency broadly fall into two categories. The first couples egocentric streams via stream concatenation, shared attention, tiling, or permutation-symmetric encodings (Enigma, 2025; Savva et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a), meaning every reference frame is itself moving, partial observation. The second improves consistency via an external state, such as an editable map with estimated per-agent poses (Po et al., 2026); while this decouples the reference from individual agent trajectories, it models spatial geometry rather than visual appearance and remains vulnerable to pose drift. In contrast, OverSeer improves consistency by introducing auxiliary streams that are jointly predicted alongside the agents streams rather than supplied as external map inputs. Efficient Video Tokenization. Modern video generators typically operate within the latent space of video VAE (Wan et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2025), with recent efficiency efforts compressing representations further via stronger tokenizers (Yu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025), token merging (Bolya et al., 2023), lightweight decoders, and bounded KV caches (Jiang et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026a). However, these generic techniques allocate computational capacity uniformly across all streams, causing an auxiliary camera view to incur nearly the same computational cost as an egocentric agent stream. closer line of work changes what latent space represents: neural video codecs encode frames relative to reference frame via residuals (Lu et al., 2019) or by conditioning (Li et al., 2021), RefTok tokenizes each frame relative to reference frame (Fan et al., 2025), and DeltaTok compresses consecutive-frame feature differences into single delta token (Kerssies et al., 2026). In these approaches, the reference frame is not fixed, but updated regularly over time, missing the advantages of OverSeers fixed views, starting from the fact that they can be compressed effectively.

Training and Inference. Knowledge of the ground-truth auxiliary visual streams is only required during training. At inference, OverSeer receives the initial agent observations and agent actions along with auxiliary camera poses. The auxiliary camera poses are sampled from scene-independent prior estimated from training poses and greedily selected to maximize field-of-view coverage without scene-specific input (see section B). The model jointly generates future agent observations and the auxiliary streams, including their initial anchor frames. Ground-truth auxiliary images are used only during training. We train OverSeer using diffusion forcing (Chen et al., 2024), where diffusion timesteps are sampled independently across temporal positions, and target latents are noised accordingly while initial conditioning frames zA remain clean. All latents, including agent latents, auxiliary anchor frames, and residual codes, are 0 projected to the same DiT hidden dimension with learnable view-identification embeddings added to each views tokens for differentiation. Agent and auxiliary streams are governed by different modalities and therefore use complementary conditioning pathways. For each agent stream, discrete actions (including agent navigation, camera motions, and inventory interactions) are formatted into short textual descriptions, encoded via frozen T5 text encoder (Raffel et al., 2020), and injected into the DiT layers through cross-attention. For each auxiliary stream, camera pose cj and its known intrinsics are converted into spatial Plücker-ray map (Sitzmann et al., 2021). These ray representations are patchified and projected into Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) (Perez et al., 2018), with scale and shift parameters to modulate the corresponding auxiliary tokens. Tokens from all agents and auxiliary streams are then jointly processed by shared self-attention layers, enabling direct cross-modality communication. We enforce causal temporal attention mask throughout the network: tokens at given temporal position can attend only to conditioning tokens and to tokens from identical t). sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We structure our experimental evaluation to test the central hypothesis of this work: extending multiagent video world model with pose-fixed, efficiently represented auxiliary views significantly improves both temporal and agent consistency compared to baselines (section 4.1). We then conduct ablation studies investigating how performance scales with the number of auxiliary views and how the δ-VAE compression ratio influences synthesis quality and computational overhead (section 4.2). For qualitative results, please refer to our website and appendix. Environments and Benchmarks. We evaluate world models by conditioning future frame rollouts on initial visual observations and multi-agent action trajectories. Primary quantitative evaluations are conducted in Minecraft, whose persistent and editable 3D world naturally tests spatial memory, multi-agent interaction, and cross-view consistency (tables 1 and 2). To evaluate long-horizon spatial reasoning, we additionally run revisit tasks in Doom  (table 2)  and showcase qualitative generalization on real-world video captures from Replay (Shapovalov et al., 2023). In Minecraft, evaluation spans two benchmark suites: 1. Solaris Benchmark (Savva et al., 2026): Evaluates five multi-agent capabilities using VLM-judged scripted questions, requiring all questions within an episode to be answered correctly. 2. MAC-Bench (Multi-Agent Consistency Benchmark): Designed specifically to evaluate world and agent consistency in harder setting. We compare OverSeer against two state-of-the-art two-player world models for Minecraft: Solaris (Savva et al., 2026) and γ-World (Liu et al., 2026a). For fair comparison, all models are evaluated with their non-distilled, causally fine-tuned checkpoints and receive identical conditioning frames and action sequences, operating strictly without auxiliary views at inference.

sections.content: FID does not reflect generation consistency. On Reunite at Start, Solaris obtains an FID of 17.06, within 3.1 points of OverSeer, yet answers none of the episodes correctly. While its generated rollouts remain visually in-distribution, they fail to reconstruct the specific scene previously left behind by the agents, frequently filling in existing craters or omitting partner agents entirely (figure 5). This disconnect demonstrates that standard frame-level distributional metrics like FID are insensitive to structural memory failures, motivating the content-level queries proposed in our new benchmark. Without shared view, agents drift apart. Both baselines enforce cross-agent agreement by coupling the agent streams directly, through concatenation or shared attention. Under this design, every reference frame is itself dynamic, partial observation, restricting agreement exclusively to moments when the agents fields of view overlap. Empirical results directly reflect this structural limitation: once agents lose visual contact, γ-World does not achieve any of the reunite tasks. The same argument accounts for the gap between Reunite at Start (60.2) and Reunite Far (37.9), as sampled cameras cover the start region more densely than the periphery. 8 Figure 5 OverSeer keeps the world consistent over time. On the three revisiting tasks (reunite at start, reunite far, dynamic event), OverSeer shows the partner and the crater where the ground truth does, while Solaris and γ-World mostly do not.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced OverSeer, multi-agent video world model that jointly generates egocentric agent views and fixed-pose auxiliary views as lightweight proxy for world-centric state. These views substantially improve consistency when agents separate and later reunite, and δ-VAE makes them cheap to model by encoding only changes relative to static reference. We hope this simple yet effective design will pave the way for world models that simulate shared environments beyond what any single agent sees.

sections.title: A Dataset Curation Pipelines
sections.content: Data. The three domains are three separate datasets, and we train one model on each. Minecraft and Doom are collected by us; the real captures are an existing dataset that we re-use in the same two-agent, many-camera arrangement. In all three, clip is 241 frames of every view at once, sampled at 20 frames per second (12 s), 576 320 per view in Minecraft and in the captures and 480 320 in Doom. Minecraft. The gameplay is collected with the Solaris engine (Savva et al., 2026): two Mineflayer bots play two-player episode on Minecraft 1.21 server and each view is recorded from real Minecraft client, so the frames are the games own graphics and every frame carries the bots ground-truth action. The bots explore by potential field, walls pushing them away and unvisited ground pulling them in, which keeps the pair moving over new terrain instead of circling one spot, and each episode is additionally labeled with one of eleven interaction modes (mining, building, fighting, chasing, exploring, reuniting and so on). We extend the engine with six fixed auxiliary cameras. They are placed in second pass: the episode is played once to establish the terrain, then the six cameras are sampled at random in the free space around the agents starting area and the episode is captured with them. Placement therefore follows the ground the episode covers rather than aiming at one point; measured over 200 episodes, camera sits median 4.9 blocks above the agents and 3.0 blocks from the nearest point of their path, tilted 52 degrees down with 70 degree field of view, and while single camera has an agent in its frustum in about half of the frames, some camera has one in 90% of them. Every view is recorded at 1280 720 and 20 frames per second. We collect 20,000 episodes of outdoor terrain and 11,000 of village worlds, 264 frames each. Doom. Doom episodes are played with Doom (ZDoom developers, 2025) on the 68 maps of Freedoom Phase 1 and Phase 2 (The Freedoom project, 2024), two marines and eight fixed auxiliary cameras per episode, and the marines are driven by the same potential-field exploration controller as the Minecraft bots. Every view is recorded at 1024 768 and 30 frames per second with 120-degree field of view. The eight cameras sit about 100 map units (3 m) above eye height, four tilted 10 degrees down and four 28 degrees, and between them they see the marines almost everywhere they walk, which is what the maps corridors and halls allow: single camera has marine in its frustum in about 85% of the frames. We train on 20,000 traversal episodes and hold out separate set of 4,000 arena episodes, in which the two marines start 128 map units apart facing each other, for evaluation. Real captures. The real sequences come from Replay (Shapovalov et al., 2023), 68 scenes of acted social interaction of about five minutes each, filmed by twelve temporally synchronized, geometrically and colorcalibrated cameras. We use eight of them in the arrangement the two games are built on: the two head-mounted cameras, which move with their wearers, are the agent views, and six static cameras are the auxiliary views. Unlike the games this gives real people, real cameras, and measured poses: every camera comes with per-frame camera-to-world pose and pinhole intrinsics; the static cameras hold still to within 5 mm and wearer covers 3 to 4 in clip. We hold out 45 clips of 241 frames, drawn from 35 of the scenes, and train on the rest of the dataset. MAC-Bench. Table 3 lists the task specifications. In all tasks, the agents begin mutually visible and lose sight of each other mid-episode. In Dynamic Event, the scripted event is placed at the midpoint between the agents and is one of sprouting crops, standing creeper, or plank cube that ignites at frame 20. Doom uses the two reunite tasks on six Freedoom maps with 1047-unit walks (32 units per block), with the partner 84 off-axis at the midpoint. We use 32 episodes per task in Minecraft and 100 per task in Doom. For VLM accuracy, Claude Opus 5 is given the generated frames and answers the task query for each agent; An episode counts as correct only if the answers for both agents match the ground truth. FID is computed between generated and ground-truth agent frames. During evaluation, accuracy is averaged over 5 independent runs of 32 episodes; episodes with failed generation or unparsable judge output are excluded. 14 Task Start Mid-episode End Query Reunite at Start 13 blocks apart, facing Reunite Far 17 blocks apart Dynamic Event 13 blocks apart, event at midpoint each wanders 9 blocks 59 blocks each, converging; partner 86 separate to 40 blocks by frame 76 exact start poses Is the partner visible? off-axis 2.9 blocks apart, facing Is the partner visible? 4.3 blocks apart What happened to the event? sections.title: B Auxiliary Camera Pose Sampling
sections.content: As described in section 3.2, OverSeer requires auxiliary camera poses in equation (3) but no auxiliary images at inference time. During training, auxiliary camera poses and their corresponding videos are provided by the dataset. At inference time, we sample the poses as follows. Scene-Independent Pose Prior. We define canonical coordinate system whose origin is the initial position of the first agent. Candidate auxiliary camera poses are sampled relative to this coordinate system from scene-independent camera-pose prior. The horizontal offset from the origin, camera height, yaw, and pitch are modeled as Gaussian variables whose parameters are estimated from the training camera poses. Camera height is constrained to be non-negative, and roll is fixed to zero. Coverage-Based Selection. We sample candidate set of poses from this prior and greedily select cameras to maximize geometric field-of-view coverage. Let Ω denote bounded discretized volume in the canonical Ω denote the cells geometrically covered by the camera frustum associated coordinate system, and let (c) (c) depends only on camera geometry and does not use scene occupancy with pose c. Since both candidate sampling and coverage computation depend only on the canonical coordinate system and camera geometry, this procedure requires no additional scene-specific visual or geometric input.

sections.title: C More Ablations
sections.content: δ-VAE PSNR dB 25.1 24.7 Minecraft Multi-agent Consistency Benchmark Reunite at Start Reunite Far Dynamic Event VLM 56.9 60.2 FID 13.47 13.99 VLM 33.4 37.9 FID 12.26 12.79 VLM 38.1 40.5 FID 17.08 17.61 Variant w/o Lalign Full δ-VAE Table 4 Ablation of the feature alignment loss. We evaluate its effect on δ-VAE reconstruction quality and downstream world consistency in Minecraft. Feature alignment loss. Table 4 ablates align. Removing it slightly improves δ-VAE reconstruction (25.1 vs. 24.7 dB PSNR) and FID, but lowers VLM accuracy on all three MAC-Bench tasks, by 2.44.5 points. Without alignment, the residual code spends its capacity on reconstructing the whole frame; with it, the code is pushed towards dynamic regions, which is what the world model needs to keep revisited scenes consistent. Reconstruction fidelity is thus not sufficient proxy for how useful compressed representation is downstream, in line with the compression trend in section 4.2.

sections.title: E Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: OverSeers benefits depend on auxiliary coverage. Regions far from the sampled cameras, as in Reunite Far, remain harder to keep consistent. Short-horizon egocentric capabilities such as movement do not benefit from auxiliary views. Aggressive residual compression also trades some fidelity and, in fast-changing scenes such as Doom, consistency for efficiency. Promising directions include adaptive or learned camera placement that follows agents into unexplored regions, auxiliary views that are re-anchored for unbounded worlds, and scaling to larger agent populations. More broadly, we hope this work encourages treating the output space of world models, meaning what they choose to render and not only what they condition on, as first-class design axis for building coherent, shared simulated worlds.

sections.title: F Prompts
sections.content: F.1 The judge Every question in both benchmarks is asked of the same judge, Claude Opus 5, in one turn: the frame or the pair of frames first, then the question, under the system prompt You are helpful assistant that evaluates Minecraft screenshots. Thinking is adaptive at low effort. The answer is reduced to its first non-empty line, lowercased and stripped of quotes and trailing punctuation, and validated by exact match against the expected word, so every prompt ends by naming the words it accepts. An episode counts as correct only if every question about it is answered correctly. Revisiting benchmark. The two reunite tasks ask only about the partner, in one sentence: Here is Minecraft/Doom screenshot. Is there another player visible on-screen? Answer with single word: "yes", "no". It is put to each agents own view at four moments read off the recorded trajectory: the first generated frame, the frame of maximum separation, the midpoint of the way back, and the rendezvous, which makes eight questions per episode. The judge sees one frame and this sentence, with no description of the task and no earlier frame, so nothing but the frame can decide the answer; the expected answer comes from the poses, the partner counting as visible when it lies well inside the view cone and within 20 blocks and as not visible when it lies outside the cone or beyond 35 blocks, with the judges own answer on the ground-truth frame standing in for the band between the two. The dynamic events add two more question shapes. The outcome question names the states the event can be in, one set per event kind; for the creeper, Here is Minecraft screenshot. What is visible where the creeper stood: creeper still standing, crater or hole blasted into the ground, or flat undamaged ground? Answer with single word from "creeper", "crater", "flat". with sprouts/wheat/none for the growing crops, intact/burning/partly burnt/gone for the burning plank cube. The progression question shows the first and the return frame together: 16 Entry Sentence forward left back right jump sneak sprint drop inv esc tab hot1hot9 swap_hands attack use mouse_turn_left mouse_turn_right mouse_look_up mouse_look_down idle The player is walking forward The player is strafing to the left The player is walking backward The player is strafing to the right The player is jumping into the air The player is sneaking and crouching down The player is sprinting and running fast The player is dropping the held item The player is opening the inventory The player is pressing escape to pause The player is switching the active hotbar tab The player is selecting item slot one . . . nine in the hotbar The player is swapping the items in both hands The player is attacking and hitting with their weapon The player is using or interacting with an object The player is turning the camera left The player is turning the camera right The player is looking up The player is looking down The player is standing still and doing nothing Table 5 The action vocabulary, one sentence per entry. The nine hotbar entries differ only in the number they name. drop, inv, esc, tab and swap_hands are never pressed in our episodes and are kept only so that the vocabulary matches the games input. Here are two Minecraft screenshots from roughly the same viewpoint, the first taken earlier and the second later. In this scene {process}. Compared with the first image, is that process further along in the second image (progressed), at the same stage (same), or at an earlier stage than in the first image (reverted)? Answer with single word: "progressed", "same", "reverted". where {process} is phrase for the event, for instance creeper explodes, disappears, and leaves crater blasted into the ground. Each event kind also has presence question asked at the first generated frame (Is there creeper (green four-legged hostile mob) visible on-screen? and its equivalents). One sentence we add. Claude reads the viewers own first-person arm in the corner of sharp frame as another player. Where that matters, we append, to every prompt and identically in both passes, The large blocky shape in the bottom-right corner is the viewers own first-person arm and held item, not another player. The prompt actually used is recorded in every result file. F.2 Action prompts Actions reach the model as language. Each of the 28 entries of the action vocabulary is written as one English sentence, encoded once by the text encoder, and stored as table of token sequences; at training and at inference the sentence of the frames action is looked up and its tokens are used as the frames conditioning context. Table 5 lists the sentences. Per frame exactly one entry is chosen. The keyboard flags score one when pressed; the mouse contributes through its yaw and pitch, whose sign picks turning left or right and looking up or down and whose magnitude is clipped to one; if nothing scores above zero, the frame is idle. The highest score wins, so frame that both walks and turns is conditioned on the stronger of the two. The conditioning frames tokens are zeroed, since it is given rather than generated, and during training the whole action context is dropped with fixed probability so that the model can be sampled with classifier-free guidance on the actions.
